## Simple explanation

XGBoost is a popular implementation of gradient-boosted decision trees. It
builds an ensemble of trees in sequence, with each new tree helping reduce
errors made by the current ensemble.

## Technical explanation

XGBoost optimizes a regularized objective using gradient and, in common
formulations, second-order information from a differentiable loss. It includes
tree construction methods, sparsity-aware handling, and systems optimizations.
Parameters control tree complexity, shrinkage, sampling, and regularization.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Boosted trees are strong baselines for structured/tabular data and support
classification, regression, ranking, and other objectives. XGBoost provides
efficient training and deployment options, but performance still depends on
valid splits, feature handling, and carefully tuned evaluation.

## How it works

Start with an initial prediction, compute loss gradients for training
examples, fit a tree to improve the objective, and add its contribution to
the ensemble. Repeat for the configured number of boosting rounds, optionally
using early stopping based on validation data.

## Practical example

For a tabular churn model, split data by customer and time if deployment
requires predicting future churn. Tune tree depth and regularization on
validation data, then report a final metric on an untouched test set.

## Common misconceptions

- XGBoost is not a neural network and does not inherently require feature
  scaling for tree splits.
- High training accuracy does not ensure generalization; leakage and
  overfitting can still occur.
